INTRODUCTION

In a world where information and data play a central role in decision-making, companies must rely on effective tools to maximize their commercial performance. In this context, a company aiming to optimize the sale of its subscriptions faces a significant challenge: despite high traffic on its website, it remains difficult to predict which recipes, among all those offered, will generate a substantial influx of visitors and positively influence sales. Indeed, it is observed that a recipe published on the site often leads to an increase in traffic, which can potentially result in a subscription sale. However, the challenge lies in identifying in advance which recipes will attract the most visitors, thereby maximizing conversion opportunities.

Leveraging the skills acquired in classification, regression, and prediction, our goal is to develop a model capable of predicting which recipes will drive high traffic. This work aims to refine the selection of popular recipes for the homepage, in order to stimulate not only website traffic but also the number of subscriptions.

2. Analysis Methodology

2.1. Data exploration and preprocessing

  • Handling Missing Values

In the presence of missing values, their relevance will be assessed based on their proportion. If the proportion is less than 5% of the entire dataset, we may remove them. Otherwise, we will apply robust methods to impute or replace the missing values.

  • Handling Outliers

    • Definition : An outlier is a data point that significantly deviates from the rest of the values in a dataset or sample. These values are considered abnormal or extreme compared to the general trend of the data.

    • Detection : Outliers can be detected using the following methods:

      • Visual methods: Box plots or scatter plots can be used to visually identify data points that lie far from the central distribution of the data.

      • Statistical methods: Interquartile Range (IQR) method: Outliers are identified as values that lie outside of the range defined by: \[ \text{Outlier} \text{ if } x < \text{Lower thd.} = Q1 - 1.5 \times IQR \text{ or } x > \text{Upper thd.} =Q3 + 1.5 \times IQR \]

        Where:

        • \(Q1\) is the first quartile (25th percentile),
        • \(Q3\) is the third quartile (75th percentile),
        • \(IQR\) is the interquartile range, \(IQR = Q3 - Q1\).

    • Correction: Winsorization with Quantiles

      There are several methods for correcting outliers, each with its advantages and disadvantages. In this project, we will focus on the Winsorization with quantiles method.

    The principle is simple: based on the thresholds defined above, we will replace the lower outlier values with the lower threshold and the higher outlier values with the upper threshold.

Function to replace Outliers with Winsorization :

# Function to replace Outliers with Winsorization 
replace_outliers <- function(x) {
  Q1 <- quantile(x, 0.25, na.rm = TRUE)
  Q3 <- quantile(x, 0.75, na.rm = TRUE)
  IQR <- Q3 - Q1
  lower_bound <- Q1 - (1.5 * IQR)
  upper_bound <- Q3 + (1.5 * IQR)
  x[x < lower_bound] <- lower_bound
  x[x > upper_bound] <- upper_bound
  return(x)
}

2.2. Univariate and Bivariate Analysis

It is important to perform descriptive analyses, which allow us to better describe and understand the structure of our data using univariate descriptive statistics, represented by tables and graphs. Additionally, it is essential to detect potential relationships between the target variable, high_traffif, and other variables in the dataset. This can be done through bivariate statistics, presented in graphs or tables, and by conducting statistical tests.

  • Tests Used

    Since our variable of interest high_traffif is categorical, we will use the following tests to examine its relationship with the explanatory variables.

    • Chi-Square Test (\(\chi^2\)) & Cramér’s V :

      The Chi-Square Test (\(\chi^2\)) will be performed to measure the relationship between the variable of interest high_traffif and the categorical explanatory variables category, servings.

      Cramér’s V : is used after a Chi-Square Test to measure the strength of the association (ranging from 0 to 1).

      • \(\mathbf{0.0 \leq V < 0.1}\) : Weak association ;
      • \(\mathbf{0.1 \leq V < 0.3}\) : Moderate association ;
      • \(\mathbf{V \geq 0.3}\) : Strong association.

    • ANOVA Test & Eta Squared (\(\eta^2\)) :

      One-way ANOVA Test is a statistical technique used to analyze the differences in means (of calories, carbohydrate, sugar, protein) between several groups high_traffic (or treatments) and determine whether these differences are statistically significant.

      Eta Squared (\(\eta^2\)) represents the proportion of the total variance of the quantitative variable that is explained by the groups (qualitative variable). It is the most common measure after an ANOVA test.

      Interpretation of Eta Squared (\(\eta^2\)) Thresholds

      • \(\mathbf{0.01 \leq \eta^2 < 0.06}\) : Small effect.
      • \(\mathbf{0.06 \leq \eta^2 < 0.14}\) : Moderate effect.
      • \(\mathbf{\eta^2 \geq 0.14}\) : Large effect.

2.3. Regression Method

We will use three models and then compare their performances to select the one that best meets the objective.

As for the models, we will use the variable high_traffif as the dependent variable and the variables calories, carbohydrate, sugar, protein, category, servings as explanatory variables. The models to be estimated are : linear probability model (LPM), logit model et Random Forest (RF) model.

These three models were chosen for their complementary strengths in analyzing a binary dependent variable. The Linear Probability Model (LPM) is simple and provides direct interpretations of coefficients as marginal effects, though it assumes linearity and may yield probabilities outside [0,1].

The Logit Model addresses these issues by modeling the relationship non-linearly using a logistic function, ensuring probabilities remain within valid bounds and allowing coefficients to be interpreted as odds ratios.

Finally, the Random Forest (RF) Model is a non-parametric approach capable of capturing complex, non-linear relationships, offering robustness to outliers and noisy data, while also providing variable importance measures. Together, these models allow for a comprehensive exploration of different methodological approaches to select the one that best meets the analysis objectives.

II. PRACTICAL PART

1. DATA PREPROCESSING

1.1 Type of Data

library(readr)
library(tidyverse) # Required packages

data <- read_csv("recipe_site_traffic_2212.csv")
glimpse(data)  # Dataset dimensions and data types
## Rows: 947
## Columns: 8
## $ recipe       <chr> "001", "002", "003", "004", "005", "006", "007", "008", "…

## $ carbohydrate <dbl> NA, 38.56, 42.68, 30.56, 1.85, 3.46, 47.95, 3.17, 3.78, 4…
## $ sugar        <dbl> NA, 0.66, 3.09, 38.63, 0.80, 1.65, 9.75, 0.40, 3.37, 3.99…
## $ protein      <dbl> NA, 0.92, 2.88, 0.02, 0.53, 53.93, 46.71, 32.40, 3.79, 11…
## $ category     <chr> "Pork", "Potato", "Breakfast", "Beverages", "Beverages", …
## $ servings     <chr> "6", "4", "1", "4", "4", "2", "4", "4", "6", "2", "1", "6…

Our dataset consists of 8 variables, including the unique recipe identifier, and contains 947 observations (recipes). In this dataset, the variables calories, carbohydrate, sugar, protein are defined as continuous quantitative variables, while recipe, category, servings, high_traffic are of class character.

However, several anomalies have been detected, which will be addressed in the following sections.

1.2 Variable Management

1.2.1 Removal of the variable recipe
data <- data %>%
  select(-recipe)

We removed the variable recipe because it is not relevant for the rest of this analysis.

1.2.2 Conversion of the variable category
table(data$category, useNA = "ifany")
## 
##      Beverages      Breakfast        Chicken Chicken Breast        Dessert 
##             92            106             74             98             83 
##   Lunch/Snacks           Meat  One Dish Meal           Pork         Potato 
##             89             79             71             84             88 
##      Vegetable 
##             83
data$category <- gsub(" Breast", "", data$category) # Remove ' Breast'

data$category <- as.factor(data$category)

table(data$category, useNA = "ifany")
## 
##     Beverages     Breakfast       Chicken       Dessert  Lunch/Snacks 
##            92           106           172            83            89 
##          Meat One Dish Meal          Pork        Potato     Vegetable 
##            79            71            84            88            83

The instructions note there should be only 10 unique values. The additional unique value stems from Chicken Breast. As Chicken is one of the possible unique values we simply removed the Breast from Chicken Breast and we converted it into a categorical variable.

1.2.3 Management of the variable High_traffic
table(data$high_traffic, useNA = "ifany")
## 
## High <NA> 
##  574  373
data$high_traffic[is.na(data$high_traffic)] <- "Low" # Replacing missing values with 'Low'

colnames(data)[colnames(data) == "high_traffic"] <- "traffic"  # Renaming the 'high_traffic' variable to 'traffic'

data$traffic <- as.factor(data$traffic) # Conversion

table(data$traffic, useNA = "ifany") # New distribution
## 
## High  Low 
##  574  373

The high_traffic variable appears to represent a traffic modality, with categories such as high indicating high traffic and low indicating low traffic. However, the missing values in this variable implicitly correspond to observations where the traffic is low. Therefore, to address these missing values, we will replace them with the low category. Additionally, to make the variable more explicit and consistent, we will rename it to high_traffic. Finally, we will convert this variable into a categorical one.

1.2.4 Management of the variable servings
table(data$servings, useNA = "ifany") # Distribution of values
## 
##            1            2            4 4 as a snack            6 6 as a snack 
##          175          183          389            2          197            1
data$servings <- gsub(" as a snack", "", data$servings) # Remove ' as a snack'

data$servings <- as.factor(data$servings) # Conversion

table(data$servings, useNA = "ifany") # New distribution
## 
##   1   2   4   6 
## 175 183 391 198

We noticed that the data in the servings column was incorrectly entered, as this variable is supposed to represent the number of servings for the recipe. To correct this issue, we will remove the value “as snack” present in the data. Furthermore, since this variable only has four distinct categories, we will convert it into a categorical variable for easier analysis.

1.3 Data Cleaning

1.3.1 Handling Duplicates
sum(duplicated(data)) # Number of duplicates
## [1] 25
data <- data[!duplicated(data), ] # Removing duplicates

We identified 25 duplicates, which have been removed from the dataset.

1.3.2 Handling Missing Values
library(VIM)

sort(colSums(is.na(data))) # Number of missing values (NA) for each column
##     category     servings      traffic     calories carbohydrate        sugar 
##            0            0            0           27           27           27 
##      protein 
##           27
# Visualize the missing values matrix
miss_matrix <- aggr(data, col = c("purple", "yellow"), 
                    numbers = TRUE, sortVars = TRUE, 
                    labels = names(data), cex.axis = 0.7, 
                    cex.numbers = 0.7, gap = 3, 
                    main = "Missing values matrix")

## 
##  Variables sorted by number of missings: 
##      Variable      Count
##      calories 0.02928416
##  carbohydrate 0.02928416
##         sugar 0.02928416
##       protein 0.02928416
##      category 0.00000000
##      servings 0.00000000
##       traffic 0.00000000
data <- data %>%
  drop_na()     #Removal of Missing Values

In each column, we identified 27 missing values, accounting for 2,9% of the total observations. By analyzing the matrix of missing values, we observed that these missing values correspond to the exact same set of rows across all columns. This redundancy indicates that the missing values are not randomly distributed but are concentrated within the same observations. Therefore, we decided to remove these 27 rows, as they represent a very small proportion of the dataset (less than 5%), and their exclusion will not impact the representativeness or quality of our analysis.

1.3.3 Outlier Management
library(reshape2)
library(patchwork)

# Boxplots before outlier correction
before_win <- ggplot(melt(data[sapply(data, is.numeric)]), aes(x = variable, y = value, fill = variable)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.colour = "red", outlier.shape = 16, outlier.size = 2) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1), legend.position = "none") +
  labs(title = "Before") +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Pastel1")

# Changing the dataset and applying the outlier correction function
data_f <- data
data_f[sapply(data, is.numeric)] <- lapply(data[sapply(data, is.numeric)], replace_outliers)

# Boxplots after outlier correction
after_win <- ggplot(melt(data_f[sapply(data_f, is.numeric)]), aes(x = variable, y = value, fill = variable)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.colour = "red", outlier.shape = 16, outlier.size = 2) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1), legend.position = "none") +
  labs(title = "After") +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Pastel1")

# Displaying both plots side by side
before_win + after_win

We identified and corrected the outliers using the Winsorization method, as outlined in the theoretical section. This approach allowed us to mitigate the impact of extreme values while preserving the integrity of the data. The processed dataset is now ready for further analysis and will be referred to as data_f.

library(effectsize)

# ANOVA Test for Categorical Variables Based on 'Traffic' and Their Eta-Squared Values

anova_calories <- aov(calories ~ traffic, data = data_f)
eta_cal <- eta_squared(anova_calories)

anova_protein <- aov(protein ~ traffic, data = data_f)
eta_pro <- eta_squared(anova_protein)

anova_carbohydrate <- aov(carbohydrate ~ traffic, data = data_f)
eta_car <- eta_squared(anova_carbohydrate)

anova_sugar <- aov(sugar ~ traffic, data = data_f)
eta_sug <- eta_squared(anova_sugar)

eta_table <- tibble(
  Variable = c("Calories", "Protein", "Carbohydrate", "Sugar"),
  Eta_Squared = c(eta_cal$Eta2, eta_pro$Eta2, eta_car$Eta2, eta_sug$Eta2)
)
eta_table
## # A tibble: 4 × 2
##   Variable     Eta_Squared
##   <chr>              <dbl>
## 1 Calories         0.00550
## 2 Protein          0.00179
## 3 Carbohydrate     0.00498
## 4 Sugar            0.00782

This difference in means is significant at the 5% level, showing a very small effect (\(\mathbf{\eta^2 = 0.00550}\)) of calorie content on traffic type determination. The higher the calorie content of a recipe, the more likely it is to generate high traffic on the site.

Therefore, this observed difference (High vs Low) is significant at the 5% level. There is a strong association between category and traffic, with a Cramér’s V of 0.583.

  • Servings by Traffic
    The graph above shows that regardless of the number of servings, traffic remains high. Specifically, 58.58% of recipes with 6 servings, 56.32% of recipes with 2 servings, 59.95% of recipes with 4 servings, and 63.78% of recipes with 6 servings generate high traffic. However, this difference (High vs Low) is not significant at the 5% level, meaning there is no association between servings and traffic.

3. MODELING

3.1 Prepare Data for Modelling

library(caret)

data_m <- data_f

# Application de la standardisation (Z-Score)
preproc <- preProcess(data_m[, sapply(data_m, is.numeric)], method = c("center", "scale"))
data_m <- predict(preproc, data_m)

data_m$traffic <- ifelse(data_m$traffic == "High", 1, 0)

set.seed(123)

train_index <- createDataPartition(data_m$traffic, p = 0.8, list = FALSE)
train <- data_m[train_index, ]
test <- data_m[-train_index, ]

control <- trainControl(method="cv", number=10) # 10-fold

To utilize the linear model, we transformed the variable traffic into a binary format, assigning 1 for High and 0 for Low. Next, we set a seed, split our dataset into training and testing sets, and finally implemented 10-fold cross-validation to be used with the random forest model.

3.2 Linear Probability Model and Logistic Regression

LPM <- lm(traffic ~ ., data = train)
logit <- glm(as.factor(traffic) ~ . , data=train, family="binomial")
3.2.1 Comparison of Marginal Effects
library(margins)

# Marginal Effects
me_logit_atmean <- mfx::logitmfx(logit, data = train, atmean = TRUE)

ME <- cbind(me_logit_atmean$mfxest[,"dF/dx"],
            coefficients(LPM)[-1])
colnames(ME) <- c("Logit marginal effect", "LPM coef")

ME_df <- as.data.frame(ME)
ME_df$Predictor <- rownames(ME_df)

ME_long <- gather(ME_df, key = "Model", value = "Effect", -Predictor)

ggplot(ME_long, aes(x = reorder(Predictor, Effect), y = Effect, fill = Model)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", position = "dodge") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(title = "Logit vs. LPM",
       x = "Predictor",
       y = "Marginal Effect") +
  theme_minimal() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("skyblue", "orange"))

In Appendix 4, we observe that only the variable category is significant at the 5% level in both models. Therefore, we will interpret the marginal effects of the different categories relative to the reference category, Beverages. At the 5% significance level, the marginal effects of the other variables are considered null in both models.

Overall, the impact of the category types relative to the Beverages category is greater in the linear model compared to the logistic model.

In fact :

  • Category Dessert (Logit vs LPM):
    Recipes in the Dessert category are 58.42 percentage points more likely to increase traffic compared to recipes in the Beverages category in the linear model, versus 40.04 percentage points in the logistic model, all else being equal.

  • Category Lunch/Snacks (Logit vs LPM):
    Recipes in the Lunch/Snacks category are 62.25 percentage points more likely to increase traffic compared to recipes in the Beverages category in the linear model, versus 40.76 percentage points in the logistic model, all else being equal.

  • Category Meat (Logit vs LPM):
    Recipes in the Meat category are 72.55 percentage points more likely to increase traffic compared to recipes in the Beverages category in the linear model, versus 42.43 percentage points in the logistic model, all else being equal.

  • Category One Dish Meal (Logit vs LPM):
    Recipes in the One Dish Meal category are 70.27 percentage points more likely to increase traffic compared to recipes in the Beverages category in the linear model, versus 40.58 percentage points in the logistic model, all else being equal.

  • Category Pork (Logit vs LPM):
    Recipes in the Pork category are 85.70 percentage points more likely to increase traffic compared to recipes in the Beverages category in the linear model, versus 44.81 percentage points in the logistic model, all else being equal.

  • Category Potato (Logit vs LPM):
    Recipes in the Potato category are 91.35 percentage points more likely to increase traffic compared to recipes in the Beverages category in the linear model, versus 47.84 percentage points in the logistic model, all else being equal.

  • Category Vegetable (Logit vs LPM):
    Recipes in the Vegetable category are 95.81 percentage points more likely to increase traffic compared to recipes in the Beverages category in the linear model, versus 50.43 percentage points in the logistic model, all else being equal.

On the other hand:

  • Category Breakfast (Logit vs LPM):
    Recipes in the Breakfast category are 28.84 percentage points more likely to increase traffic compared to recipes in the Beverages category in the linear model, versus 35.62 percentage points in the logistic model, all else being equal.

  • Category Chicken (Logit vs LPM):
    Recipes in the Chicken category are 39.58 percentage points more likely to increase traffic compared to recipes in the Beverages category in the linear model, versus 42.59 percentage points in the logistic model, all else being equal.

3.2.1 Comparison of VarImp (t-values)
z_values <- cbind(me_logit_atmean$mfxest[, "z"],
                  summary(LPM)$coefficients[, "t value"][-1])
colnames(z_values) <- c("logit", "LPM")

z_df <- as.data.frame(z_values)
z_df$Predictor <- rownames(z_df)
z_long <- gather(z_df, key = "Model", value = "Effect", -Predictor)

ggplot(z_long, aes(x = reorder(Predictor, Effect), y = Effect, fill = Model)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", position = "dodge") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(title = "Logit vs. LPM",
       x = "Predictor",
       y = "VarImp") +
  theme_minimal() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("skyblue", "orange"))

The graph above shows that the same categories are equally important for both the linear model (LPM) and the logistic model (Logit). However, in general, the importance of these categories is higher for the logistic model. Other variables have no significant importance.

Indeed, under the reference category Beverages, the category Vegetable has the greatest importance in driving high traffic, with a VarImp of 13.98 for the logistic model compared to 13.46 for the LPM. Next is the category Meat, with a VarImp of 9.70 for the logistic model versus 9.31 for the LPM, followed by Lunch/Snacks, Dessert, Chicken, and Breakfast, which have respective VarImp values of 9.04, 8.76, 6.24, and 5.61 for the logistic model compared to 8.39, 7.78, 5.77, and 4.26 for the LPM.

However, for the categories Potato and Pork, the importance is higher for the LPM, with respective VarImp values of 12.57 and 10.93, compared to 11.71 and 10.68 for the logistic model.

In conclusion, the category type is the only strong indicator for predicting traffic increase in both models.

3.3 Random Forest (RF) model

3.3.1 Variable Importance Scores.
rf_mod <- train(as.factor(traffic) ~ . , data=train, method="ranger", trControl=control, metric = "Accuracy")

#Fit the best model
rf_aju <- ranger::ranger(as.factor(traffic) ~ . , data=train, mtry=rf_mod$bestTune$mtry,importance="impurity",probability = TRUE)

varimp <- tibble(Variable=names(rf_aju$variable.importance),
                 Importance = rf_aju$variable.importance) %>%
  arrange(desc(Importance)) %>%
  mutate(Variable=factor(Variable, levels=Variable[order(Importance)]))

ggplot(varimp, aes(x = Variable, y = Importance, fill = Variable)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", position = "dodge") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(title = "Random Forest",
       x = "Predictor",
       y = "VarImp") +
  theme_minimal()

The variable category is by far the most important (Importance = 98.6) in the Random Forest model, indicating that it plays a key role in predictions. Nutritional variables such as protein (48.4), calories (38.9), carbohydrate (36.1), and sugar (35) also have a notable but lesser impact, while servings has much lower importance (10.5), suggesting it has little influence on the results. In summary, categories dominate the explanation of the target, followed by nutritional factors.

3.3 Performance

3.3.1 Prediction Using LPM, Logit, and Random Forest Models on Test Data
test$prob_lpm <- predict(LPM, newdata = test)

test$prob_logit <- predict(logit, newdata = test, type = "response")

test$prob_rf <- predict(rf_aju, test, type = "response")$predictions[,2]

The predicted probabilities for each model have been added to the test dataset.

test$index <- predict(logit, test, type = "link") # the linear index : beta*X_i

test %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = index, y = traffic)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_rug(data = test %>% filter(traffic == 0), mapping = aes(x = index),
           color = "orange", sides = "b", alpha = .5) +
  geom_rug(data = test %>% filter(traffic == 1), mapping = aes(x = index),
           color = "orange", sides = "t", alpha = .5) +
  geom_line(aes(y = prob_lpm, color = "LPM", linetype = "LPM"), lwd = 1) +
  geom_line(aes(y = prob_rf, color = "Random Forest", linetype = "Random Forest"), lwd = 1) +
  geom_line(aes(y = prob_logit, color = "Logit", linetype = "Logit"), lwd = 1) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Logit" = "blue", "LPM" = "red", "Random Forest" = "green")) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c("Logit" = "solid", "LPM" = "dashed", "Random Forest" = "dotdash")) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(y = "Probability",color = "Models", linetype = "Models") +
  theme(legend.position = "top") +
  theme_bw()

The graph above shows that the predicted values from the Logit and Random Forest models are correctly within the [0, 1] range, whereas some predictions from the LPM (4 predictions) have probabilities greater than 1.

3.3.2 ROC & AUC
library(pROC)

roc_lpm <- roc(test$traffic, test$prob_lpm)

roc_logit <- roc(test$traffic, test$prob_logit)

roc_rf <- roc(test$traffic, test$prob_rf)

plot(roc_lpm, col = "blue", main = "ROC Curves", 
     xlab = "1 - Specificity", ylab = "Sensitivity", 
     lwd = 2)
plot(roc_logit, col = "red", add = TRUE, lwd = 2)
plot(roc_rf, col = "green", add = TRUE, lwd = 2)
legend("bottomright", legend = c("LPM", "Logit", "Random Forest"), 
       col = c("blue", "red", "green"), lwd = 2, cex = 0.8)

auc_lpm <- auc(roc_lpm)

auc_logit <- auc(roc_logit)

auc_rf <- auc(roc_rf)

AUC <- tibble(
  Model = c("Logit", "LPM", "Random Forest"),
  auc = c(auc_logit, auc_lpm, auc_rf)
)

ggplot(AUC, aes(x = Model, y = auc , fill = Model)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", width = 0.6) +
  labs(x = "Model", y = "AUC") +
  theme_minimal() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("skyblue", "orange", "lightgreen"))

We observe that the AUC of the Logit model is the highest at 84.8%, meaning that the Logit model has an 85% chance of correctly classifying a positive observation compared to a negative one. This is slightly higher than the LPM (84.5%) and the Random Forest model (81.6%). AUC is a good indicator to use given the imbalance in our data.

The goal is to predict which recipes will generate high traffic, so we will prioritize maximizing sensitivity while maintaining a reasonable specificity. Our target is to achieve a sensitivity of around 90%. In Appendix 5, we provide the cutoff values, sensitivity, and specificity for each model. The results meeting our objective are as follows:

  • LPM: threshold = 0.4202; Sensitivity = 0.9048; Specificity = 0.6216
  • Logit: threshold = 0.4120; Sensitivity = 0.9143; Specificity = 0.6216
  • RF: threshold = 0.4024; Sensitivity = 0.9048; Specificity = 0.4730

Therefore, we have determined the classification thresholds for each model, as we cannot use the standard (0.5) threshold due to the data imbalance.

test$class_lpm <- ifelse(test$prob_lpm > 0.42, 1, 0)

test$class_logit <- ifelse(test$prob_logit > 0.412, 1, 0)

test$class_rf <- ifelse(test$prob_rf > 0.402, 1, 0)
3.3.3 Confusion matrice and accuracy
confusion_lpm <- table(test$class_lpm,test$traffic,
                       dnn=c("prediction_LPM","truth"))

confusion_logit <- table(test$class_logit,test$traffic,
                       dnn=c("prediction_Logit","truth"))

confusion_rf <- table(test$class_rf,test$traffic,
                         dnn=c("prediction_RF","truth"))

confusion_lpm
##               truth
## prediction_LPM  0  1
##              0 46 10
##              1 28 95
confusion_logit
##                 truth
## prediction_Logit  0  1
##                0 46  9
##                1 28 96
confusion_rf
##              truth
## prediction_RF  0  1
##             0 33 13
##             1 41 92
# for LPM
precision_lpm <- posPredValue(as.factor(test$class_lpm), as.factor(test$traffic), positive = "1")
recall_lpm <- sensitivity(as.factor(test$class_lpm), as.factor(test$traffic), positive = "1")
f1_lpm <- (2 * precision_lpm * recall_lpm) / (precision_lpm + recall_lpm)

# for Logit
precision_logit <- posPredValue(as.factor(test$class_logit), as.factor(test$traffic), positive = "1")
recall_logit <- sensitivity(as.factor(test$class_logit), as.factor(test$traffic), positive = "1")
f1_logit <- (2 * precision_logit * recall_logit) / (precision_logit + recall_logit)

# For Random Forest
precision_rf <- posPredValue(as.factor(test$class_rf), as.factor(test$traffic), positive = "1")
recall_rf <- sensitivity(as.factor(test$class_rf), as.factor(test$traffic), positive = "1")
f1_rf <- (2 * precision_rf * recall_rf) / (precision_rf + recall_rf)

metrics <- tibble(
  Model = c("LPM", "Logit", "Random Forest"),
  Precision = c(precision_lpm, precision_logit, precision_rf),
  Recall = c(recall_lpm, recall_logit, recall_rf),
  F1_Score = c(f1_lpm, f1_logit, f1_rf)
)

metrics
## # A tibble: 3 × 4
##   Model         Precision Recall F1_Score
##   <chr>             <dbl>  <dbl>    <dbl>
## 1 LPM               0.772  0.905    0.833
## 2 Logit             0.774  0.914    0.838
## 3 Random Forest     0.692  0.876    0.773

-The logistic regression model (Logit) demonstrates superior overall performance with an accuracy of 0.774, a recall of 0.914, and an F1 score of 0.838. This indicates that it successfully identifies most high-traffic cases (high recall) while maintaining a good balance between precision and recall.

  • The LPM model closely follows with an accuracy of 0.772, a recall of 0.905, and an F1 score of 0.833. Although slightly behind the Logit model, it remains effective in predicting positive cases while minimizing errors.

  • The Random Forest model, while having a high recall (0.905), shows a lower accuracy (0.709) and an F1 score of 0.795. This suggests that it generates more false positives, reducing its ability to provide reliable predictions for positive values (high traffic).

In conclusion, while both Random Forest and LPM capture positive cases well, the Logit model offers a better trade-off between precision, recall, and F1 score, making it more suitable for this task in this specific context.

3.4 Final Model & Recommendations

3.4.1 Final Model : Logit model

In the Logit model, only the variable category is significant at the 5% level, with a VarImp of 13.98. Overall, the impact of different categories relative to the Beverages category is substantial. Specifically, recipes in the Vegetable category are 50.43 percentage points more likely to drive traffic compared to those in the Beverages category. Following closely, recipes in the Potato category are 47.84 percentage points more likely to increase traffic. On the other hand, recipes in the Dessert, Lunch/Snacks, Meat, One Dish Meal, Pork, and Chicken categories show traffic increases ranging from 45% to 40%. Meanwhile, recipes in the Breakfast category are 35.62 percentage points more likely to generate traffic compared to those in the Beverages category.

Thus, the category variable emerges as the best predictor of high traffic.

This Logit model excels at detecting positive cases (high traffic), achieving an accuracy of 0.774, a recall of 0.914, and an F1 score of 0.838.

3.4.1 Recommendations

To assist the company in predicting high-traffic recipes, we recommend deploying the Logistic Regression model into production. This model demonstrates robust performance with an F1 score of 83.8%, indicating a good balance between accuracy (77.4%) and recall (91.4%).

In practice, this means the model can efficiently identify most recipes likely to generate high traffic while minimizing false alarms (false positives). By implementing this model, approximately 83.8% of predictions will guarantee high traffic, which will increase the Product Manager’s confidence in identifying high-potential recipes.

We emphasize that categories with a significant impact on traffic should be prioritized when creating new recipes or promoting existing ones.

CONCLUSION

The recipe analysis highlighted the factors influencing high traffic on the site. Through a methodical approach combining descriptive analysis, inferential statistics, and modeling, a thorough inspection revealed a low percentage of missing values (2.9%), which were removed. Logistic regression proved to be a robust tool for predicting high traffic for recipes. With an F1 score of 83.8%, this model provides a good compromise between accuracy (77.4%) and recall (91.4%), ensuring effective detection of high-potential recipes while limiting false positives. This model stands out for its ability to guide the company in identifying the most promising recipes, enabling informed decision-making. Therefore, the logistic regression model can be integrated into existing systems to provide real-time predictions and guide decisions on recipe publication and promotion.
